prompt: An enrolment table has student id `sid`, course code `cid`, student name `sname`, course title `ctitle` and `grade`. Which proposed dependency is a **trivial FD**, one that holds in every relation whatever the business rules?

options.text: The student id and course code together determine the course code
options.explanation: Correct. The right side (course code) is already part of the left side, so any two rows that agree on the left side automatically agree on it. It holds in every relation and tells you nothing.

options.text: The student id and course code together determine the grade
options.explanation: Non-trivial: grade is not among the left-hand attributes, so this states a real business rule (one grade per student per course).

options.text: The student id determines the student name
options.explanation: Non-trivial: the name is not part of the id, so this is a real rule that data could break.

options.text: The course code determines both the course code and the course title
options.explanation: Not trivial, because the title is not on the left. Its course-code part is trivial, but the dependency as a whole makes a real claim.

workedExample:
A dependency is trivial exactly when everything on its right side already appears on its left side.

1. Course code from (student id, course code): course code is on the left. **Trivial.**
2. Grade from (student id, course code): grade is new. Non-trivial.
3. Name from student id: name is new. Non-trivial.
4. Code and title from code: the title is new, so the whole rule is non-trivial.

Trivial dependencies come free from Armstrong's reflexivity rule and never need enforcing.

prompt:
A table currently holds these synthetic test rows, including a deliberately inconsistent M1/Leeds entry. Treat the listed values as data to audit, rather than a claim about postal geography:

```
zip    city      street
SW1A   London    Mall
SW1A   London    Horse Gds
M1     Manchstr  Oxford Rd
M1     Leeds     Albion St
```

Which statement about these proposed functional dependencies, as constraints on all legal states, is justified by this data alone?

options.text: The postcode district fixes the city as a valid business rule
options.explanation: The two M1 rows agree on zip but disagree on city, so this FD is violated here (or the data is dirty).

options.text: The business rule that city determines zip is proved by these rows
options.explanation: The data contains no counterexample, but a lack of counterexamples never proves an FD. It is a rule only if the business says so.

options.text: The business rule that street determines zip is proved because every street here is different
options.explanation: Unique values in a sample do not make an FD a rule; two towns can each have an Oxford Road.

options.text: The data refutes the postcode-to-city dependency: equal districts have different cities
options.explanation: Correct. The two M1 rows have the same postcode-district value but different city values, refuting that dependency on this stored state.

workedExample:
1. To refute a functional dependency, find two relational tuples equal on its determinant but different on its right side.
2. Both M1 rows agree on zip ('M1') but disagree on city ('Manchstr' and 'Leeds'), so the postcode-to-city rule is violated in this stored state.
3. For the proposed city-to-district and street-to-district rules there is no counterexample, but that is all you can say. Data can disprove an FD, never prove one.
4. In practice: either the FD is a genuine rule and a row is wrong (fix it), or the FD was never true (do not design around it).

prompt: A colleague argues: “If a student and course together fix the grade, the student alone must fix it too.” Which tiny instance shows this inference is invalid? Tuples are written (sid, cid, grade).

options.explanation: Correct. The student/course pairs differ, so the premise is satisfied; the student is the same and grades differ, so the student-alone conclusion fails.
These are the same relational tuple (a relation is a set), and they agree on everything, so nothing is violated.
These have different students, so they do not refute the student-alone conclusion.
The student/course pair is the same but grades differ, so this violates the premise itself.

workedExample:
To refute an inference, construct a relation satisfying its premise but violating its conclusion.

1. Premise: each student/course pair has one grade.
2. Target: same student, different grades on different courses.
3. Use two different courses so the premise is not violated:

```
sid cid grade
 1  DB   A
 1  AI   B
```

4. The premise holds, the target fails, so the inference is invalid. The left side of an FD cannot be split.
